PRESS RELEASE October 27, 2026

Apple introduces
the new 14‑inch 
MacBook Pro with M6

Supercharged by M6, the 14-inch MacBook Pro features incredible performance and next-level AI capabilities, enhanced connectivity, and up to 24 hours of battery life, delivering even more value
CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6, delivering even more performance, powerful on-device AI capabilities, and faster connectivity for college students, business users, creators, and more. M6 features an advanced 12-core CPU with the world’s fastest CPU core, so everything from productivity tasks to more demanding pro workflows feels incredibly fast and responsive.1 The 12-core GPU delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics and up to 25 percent faster AI workloads when compared to M5, making the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 a compelling value for users who need serious power.2 For those upgrading from M1, the performance gains are even more significant, with up to 11x faster graphics and up to 13x faster AI performance.3 With additional Neural Accelerators in the GPU and a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, M6 turns MacBook Pro into an even more powerful platform for AI — from taking advantage of Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features across apps and macOS to running LLMs locally, all while preserving user privacy.4 In addition, the 14-inch MacBook Pro features Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, while superfast storage makes working with large files, exporting projects, and running demanding AI workflows fly. And with phenomenal battery life of up to 24 hours, it delivers the same remarkable performance whether plugged in or on battery, so users can work, create, and pursue their passions from anywhere.3 It also offers the advanced features users love, including the stunning Liquid Retina XDR display with a nano-texture option, a 12MP Center Stage camera, an immersive six-speaker sound system, and a wide array of ports. Together with macOS 27, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is a major upgrade for existing Mac users and those coming to Mac for the first time. Available in space black and silver, it can be pre-ordered beginning tomorrow, October 28, with availability starting Friday, November 6.
“The 14-inch MacBook Pro is the pro laptop of choice for a wide range of users — from college students, to business professionals across every industry, to multidisciplinary creators doing it all on one device,” said Shelly Goldberg, Apple’s vice president of Hardware Engineering. “With the powerful M6 chip, we’re taking performance to the next level, with a boost in CPU speed and graphics and even more powerful capabilities for on-device AI. With its amazing battery life, remarkable Liquid Retina XDR display, and even faster connectivity, the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 delivers a fantastic combination of performance, capability, and value.”

M6: Blazing-Fast Performance and On-Device AI Capabilities

M6 brings even more performance and next-level AI capabilities to the 14-inch MacBook Pro. Featuring a powerful 12-core CPU, a 12-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in each core, Dual 16-core Neural Engine, and faster unified memory, MacBook Pro with M6 is faster and more responsive.
The 12-core CPU, with two more cores than before, brings blazing-fast single- and multithreaded performance, so users can fly through everything from multitasking across apps to compiling code to handling complex creative workflows. The 12-core GPU, also with two additional cores, delivers up to 30 percent faster graphics performance when compared to M5.2 Everything from 3D modeling to photo editing and gaming feels incredibly fast, enhanced by a third-generation ray-tracing engine and Dynamic Caching to optimize on-chip memory. It also brings up to 25 percent faster performance for on-device AI workloads, like LLM prompt processing, compared to M5.3 The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers up to 1.9x faster performance than M5 and works with the advanced GPU to dramatically accelerate AI workloads like image generation, Super Resolution, and AI upscaling.2 The Neural Engine also powers Apple Intelligence, enabling advanced and energy-efficient on-device AI processing. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 does all this with industry-leading performance per watt and up to 24 hours of battery life, the longest ever in a Mac. With 16GB of unified memory standard, configurable up to 32GB, and higher memory bandwidth up to 170GB/s, MacBook Pro makes multitasking and working with demanding apps and large projects even faster.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 helps motion designers model 3D objects, design product visualizations, and render animations with ease.
The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 enables:3
  • Up to 13x faster time to first token performance for LLM prompt processing compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
  • Up to 11.7x faster render performance with ray tracing in Blender compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
  • Up to 3.3x faster image-processing performance in Affinity compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.2x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
  • Up to 2.5x faster project build performance when compiling code in Xcode compared to the 13-inch MacBook Pro with M1, and up to 1.3x faster than the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5.
  • A project is edited in Adobe After Effects on a 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6.
  • An image is edited in the Pixelmator Pro app on the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6.
  • Lines of code are compiled in Xcode on the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6.

A Huge Upgrade with Even More Value

There’s never been a better time for customers to upgrade from a previous-generation MacBook Pro with Apple silicon or an Intel-based Mac. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 delivers remarkable value thanks to major performance improvements and powerful AI capabilities. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro also features all of the compelling capabilities that have made it so popular, including:
  • Phenomenal battery life: In addition to the huge leap in performance, battery life gets up to 14 additional hours for Intel-based upgraders and up to four more hours for users coming from M1, delivering up to 24 hours overall, so users can get more done on a single charge. Users coming from Intel-based and M1 systems will also get 16GB of starting unified memory, an additional Thunderbolt port, and the space black finish with an anodization seal for fewer fingerprints.
  • A brilliant pro display: The stunning Liquid Retina XDR display delivers up to 1600 nits of peak HDR brightness and a 1,000,000:1 contrast ratio, bringing HDR photos and videos to life with deep blacks, brilliant highlights, and vibrant colors. And for users working in bright or challenging lighting conditions, a nano-texture display option dramatically reduces reflections and glare.
  • Powerful connectivity: Now with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, the 14-inch MacBook Pro delivers fast wireless performance and low latency, along with support for up to two external displays. Its versatile array of ports — including the HDMI, MagSafe 3, and three Thunderbolt 4 ports; an SDXC card slot; and a headphone jack — makes it easy to connect high-speed peripherals, transfer photos, or expand a workspace.
  • Advanced camera, mics, and speakers: A 12MP Center Stage camera with Desk View helps keep users perfectly framed on video calls, while a studio-quality three-mic array and amazing six-speaker sound system with Spatial Audio deliver an immersive audio experience.
  • Fast charging: MacBook Pro with M6 supports fast charging, reaching up to 50 percent charge in just 30 minutes when paired with a compatible higher-wattage USB-C power adapter, such as the 96W Power Adapter.3
  • A laptop that’s built to last: With an enclosure made from 100 percent recycled aluminum, MacBook Pro is exceptionally durable and can stand up to everyday use for years to come.
  • Better together with iPhone: When used together with Continuity, iPhone and Mac are even more powerful — letting users move seamlessly across devices to share files and photos, hand off tasks, and even control their iPhone from their 14-inch MacBook Pro.5 Users switching to Mac for the first time can use iPhone to conveniently and securely transfer settings, files, photos, passwords, and more.
  • The Liquid Retina XDR display is showcased on the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6.
  • Two sides of the new 14-inch MacBook Pro show the laptop’s array of ports.

macOS 27 Golden Gate

The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 comes to life with macOS 27, which includes Siri AI, a profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal assistant; helpful Apple Intelligence features across everyday apps; and improvements that make the Mac even more responsive and reliable. Siri AI can draw on personal context to help users find what they need in the moment across messages, emails, photos, and more; answer questions about virtually any topic; and get things done across apps — all with groundbreaking privacy protections. Siri AI is integrated into Spotlight and systemwide context menus, and users can ask Siri about what’s on their display with Visual Intelligence using a dedicated keyboard shortcut. Users can also write and edit with Siri almost anywhere they type.
Additionally, Apple Intelligence makes apps smarter and more useful. In Safari, it powers new tools that automatically organize a user’s tabs into topics; notify them of website changes, like product restocks or price drops; and enable the creation of custom extensions based on a description. Users can also easily create an automation in Shortcuts by simply describing it, or tap into intelligent photo editing tools in the Photos app. The new 14-inch MacBook Pro gets even more responsive, reliable, and delightful with refinements to design, performance, search, and more. Updates to Liquid Glass deliver an even more focused and approachable experience. A new slider in Settings gives users the option to personalize Liquid Glass, adjusting it anywhere from ultraclear to fully tinted to match their preference, and app icons are sharper and more defined.

14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 and the Environment

The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 was built with the environment in mind and drives progress toward Apple’s ambitious plan to be carbon neutral across its entire footprint by 2030. It is made with 45 percent recycled content overall,6 including 100 percent recycled aluminum in the enclosure, 100 percent recycled cobalt in the battery, and, in a first for Apple, 100 percent recycled tantalum in multiple capacitors. It is manufactured with 60 percent renewable electricity, such as wind and solar, across the supply chain. The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 is designed to be durable and repairable, and meets Apple’s high standards for energy efficiency and safe chemistry. As with all Apple products, its paper packaging is 100 percent fiber-based7 and designed to be recycled.
  • Customers can pre-order the new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starting tomorrow, October 28, on apple.com/store and in the Apple Store app in 35 countries and regions, including the U.S. It will begin arriving to customers, and in Apple Store locations and Apple Authorized Resellers, starting Friday, November 6.
  • The 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 starts at $1,999 (U.S.) and $1,899 (U.S.) with education savings. Additional technical specifications and configure-to-order options are available at apple.com/macbook-pro.
  • With Apple Upgrade, eligible customers in the U.S. can lease a new Mac with low monthly payments and easily upgrade at the end of their lease.8 Lease the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 with Apple Upgrade from $38.99 (U.S.) per month, excluding taxes and any trade-in credit, for 36 months.^
  • With Apple Trade In, customers can trade in their current computer and get credit toward a new Mac. Customers can visit apple.com/shop/trade-in to see what their device is worth. item.title: Software may be getting worse, but it used to be horrible (293 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://www.bitlog.com/2026/10/27/software-may-be-getting-worse-but-it-used-to-be-horrible/, See on Hacker News

Software is degrading all around us, for obvious reasons. I've written about this before. All else equal, if you increase your code production by 10x but you don't reduce your error rate by a factor of 10, then your production app is buggier than it used to be.

I've seen threads where people also have some nostalgia for the past: "software used to be better in the past" or "we've forgotten how to program like we used to" or "software quality has been declining for decades." And as someone who has used computers since 1990, I'm here to disabuse you of this notion. Software was horrible. Everything crashed all the time. Yes, there were great programmers like John Carmack who could keep the entire program in their head and iterate on thoughtful codebases over decades. No, they did not write a majority of the software that we used to use.

Historical context

Almost everyone in the world was on Windows. Windows peaked around a 95% market share, plus or minus a few percentage points based on your source. Yes, you probably knew someone with an iMac who would tell you that it was way better than a Windows machine, and they could prove it if anyone ever actually released applications for Macs. And yes, there were Linux distros like Debian where people could get real computing done[0].

But those were exceptions. Almost every computer user had a Windows machine and either an Intel or an AMD processor. And Windows had a lot of problems.

There was one saving grace though: companies only got one chance to ship their software. At a certain point, it was going to be loaded onto a floppy disk or burned onto a CD or a ROM, put into a box, and mailed out. And that version had to work out of the box. So there was some quality floor that you couldn't slip below.

How bad did it get?

Here's a collection of things that I remember. This isn't linear; it's my collection of memories from 1990 and onward.

Blue Screen of Death

Windows had extreme stability issues for most of my childhood.

Let me introduce you to the song of my people, the Blue Screen of Death.

This was Windows' version of a kernel panic. It happened right when you were in the middle of something. Or maybe you were doing nothing. It didn't matter: the blue screen was coming.

Your computer crashed for a lot of reasons. First, device drivers. If you bought some new peripheral like a joystick, it'd come with a floppy disk or CD with device drivers. You'd dutifully install them. The device drivers had the same function as they do today: they help the operating system understand how to interface with the hardware. This might get you thinking, "Oh wow, so they sent out the device drivers on physical media? You can't update a physical disk once you ship it. Surely they took extra care to get everything right." My friend, this could not be further from the truth. I'm sure there were good drivers and bad drivers. But in aggregate, they were buggy, and it only took one marginal device driver to destabilize your computer.

The Windows operating system also had its own code quality issues back then, and would sometimes fail to fully reclaim resources from programs that exited. So your computer would slowly degrade over time until eventually the slow rot would take down your machine.

All in all, your computer would just blink out of existence from time to time. It was a fact of life.

Autosave

Do you know what pairs really well with a computer that crashes all the time? Applications that don't autosave. Even better, applications with autosave that don't flush buffered writes and corrupt their save files.

It was commonplace to get into the zone and work on a document for hours, and then suddenly you would get either a Blue Screen of Death, or a pop-up saying that your application had a problem and had to exit. And you'd scream and you'd double-click your document over and over, but it was no use. You had to start over. But there was a consolation prize. It was your turn to tell everyone, "I was working on a document for THREE HOURS! And then the computer crashed and I lost everything. It was all gone. I had to redo it." There was always that one asshole that was like "why didn't you save?" But you didn't get mad. You knew that he was 2 weeks from having the same thing happen to him.

When I joined the Google Docs team back in 2010, we instrumented the Ctrl+s keyboard shortcut for fun. It didn't do anything but record a metric saying that it had been pressed. This "save" keyboard shortcut was in the top 5 non-editing user actions, just behind things like "move the cursor with arrow keys." And it did absolutely nothing. Google Docs autosaves. But everyone was so traumatized from years or decades of losing work that they reflexively saved anytime they edited anything.

Nothing was secure

When my sister and I were little, we loved going into stores with display units. The computers would often have games installed you could play. Worst case, you could always open up MS Paint or Solitaire and mess around for a few minutes.

One time, we were in a store where the display models had password-protected screensavers. My sister was undeterred. She just hit Ctrl+Alt+Del, selected the screensaver application, and clicked "End Task." And we were in. The best minds of Microsoft were nothing next to the hacking talent of a 9-year-old.

And this is the level of security that your computer afforded you. If you used the Internet for long enough, your computer would start to collect a bunch of advertising malware. When you turned your computer on, you would start to see pop-ups and pop-unders with random ads, even when you weren't using browsers. So you'd do another antivirus scan, or later on you could visit websites that could also run the malware scans for you.

And not to mention the viruses that would drop the Internet to its knees once a year by doing trivial things like "adding a macro to a Word document that sends emails."

Disk fragmentation

Any techie can remember going to a nontechnical relative's house. In some dusty corner, they'd have an ancient Windows computer barely hanging on by a thread. It would literally take 20 minutes to turn on.

You'd sigh and say, "let me fix this for you."

You would open two programs. This would take about 5 minutes. The first program emptied cache files and the Recycle Bin. The second was Disk Defragmenter.

Back in the day, hard drives in Wintel boxes stored data with spinning magnetic platters. The hard drive had a retractable arm with a little magnetic reader, and it would read data by retracting the arm to the right position and then moving the disk to the start of a sector.

But of course, as you add more and more files, the game of Tetris doesn't work, and the rest of your file doesn't neatly fit onto the disk before the next file's record begins. So your file would end up in two (or more) places on the hard drive. This was called fragmentation. A little bit of fragmentation was unavoidable, but if more and more files became fragmented then your computer became slower and slower until eventually Grandpa's computer took 20 minutes to start.

Many modern filesystems, Windows' included, automatically handle defragmentation in the background nowadays. But Windows did not back then. You needed to periodically manually start the defragmentation process yourself.

By the time I got into college, I discovered that Windows had a scheduler and could run Disk Defragmenter whenever I wanted, so I just left my computer on all the time and let it defragment at 5 in the morning.

Phenomenal cosmic power, itty bitty memory

Applications were heavily memory constrained, so programmers tried to save bits and bytes everywhere.

This should have been invisible to me, but it wasn't.

At one point I had a crappy video game version of Axis and Allies for the PC, released in 1998[1]. Imagine Risk but World War 2. And the AI was really bad, and could generally be beaten easily. But the game had a major flaw: If a country had more than 255 units, the whole game would crash. And naturally the AI also loved to turtle, so it was common for the AI to have a territory with over a hundred units that was impossible to wear down. So because of this programming choice, the game was a race to wipe out the enemy before it could force a stalemate by crashing the game.

This kind of thing happened all the time. During my first programming class in my freshman year of high school, one of our lessons was effectively, "here's why you all recognize numbers like 128, 256, and maybe 65536."

Software came on unreliable physical media

Even if the software worked perfectly, you might scratch your game CD and lose the ability to play it. Then you'd start asking your friends if anyone had a spare copy of Red Alert or something, just so that you could finally finish the single-player campaign.

This wasn't unique to CDs. Anything physical could degrade. My half-brother had a NES game called Dragon Warrior or something, but the cartridge was corrupted and there was no way to leave the first room. And even if you kept all of your games in good condition, the contacts inside of the NES that connected the cartridge to the console could rust and fail. This kind of thing happened all the time.

"But Jake, that's hardware and not software." All I'm saying is that your software was fragile and it needed to be protected and preserved. It's not like you had the option for a physical disk or the online install and you chose the disk. By the nature of distribution, the software itself would degrade and rot away from you.

Online games assumed good behavior

One of the earliest online games I played was Diablo II, which means that I have seen the true heart of darkness inside of humanity.

Online games have a strange problem: gamers often don't want to be together. They just happen to cohabitate a space. And Diablo II had a lot of design features that lent themselves to chaos:

  • There were rampant client-side hacks. In PVP servers, people would use hacks to e.g. fire tracking arrows far beyond the range that they should have been able to.

  • All item drops were equally available to everyone in the server. That means when you got close to killing an act boss, you and your party would transition from allies to rivals and spam click when the boss finally popped.

  • If you had a corpse on the ground and died again, you'd lose everything you had equipped. People would try to force you to have a full inventory by dropping a bunch of cheap items onto your corpse, hoping that you'd accidentally pick up common items before picking up your corpse. Then you'd try to pick up your corpse. You'd only pick up some of the items. Then they'd kill you a second time and you'd lose everything that you managed to pick up.

  • The game had a lot of item duping glitches. As you can imagine, this ruined the in-game economy since it became dominated by the duped items. And it enabled a lot of scams. They'd pretend that they just duped an item, and they'd wait for someone to ask how they did it. Then they'd walk the user through step-by-step, but one step would involve dropping your item on the ground and then the scammer would pick up the item.

  • There was no guild system, but people still ran guilds. This means that there was no trusted way to identify guaranteed friendlies.

Many of these were fixed by the time Diablo III came around. They had extra guards against duplicated items. Bosses gave players individual drops, so there was no competition for items when you killed bosses. And you didn't need to recover items from your corpse in a way that risked you losing items. These were all hard-won lessons.

Turbo button

I started using my family's computer around 1990 when I learned how to read. The computer was a beige 286 that sat on our desk with the monitor perched on top. It had a 5.25" floppy drive. It had a power button. It had a reset button. And it had a TURBO button. The TURBO button was supposed to be ignored most of the time, but you could press it when you needed to slow the computer's processor down.

Why would you need to do that? Because IBM's first desktop computers ran on the 8088 processor at 4.77MHz[2]. It didn't stay this way for long. But there was a problem: many programmers wrote their applications with the assumption that computers had that 4.77MHz processor. Programmers synchronized animations, video game frame rates, and generally relied on the assumption that they were working with a fixed clock speed. If you used one of these applications on a faster processor, they would likely be unusable.

Computer manufacturers devised a simple solution: add a TURBO button that would just slow your CPU down on demand. Whenever you ran into an application that had timing issues, just press that TURBO button and watch it slow down to a comfortable speed.

I never needed to actually press the TURBO button in anger. My understanding is that most of the applications that benefitted from the TURBO button were games, and we only played newer educational games that didn't have these timing issues. When editing this post, I thought about dropping this section a few times. But can you imagine having an "Original iPhone" button on the side of your iPhone so that the Notes app could work? Good grief.

Modern software isn't perfect

Modern software isn't perfect. It's bloated. It's slow. It was written by too many people. It's too complex. It has too many cooks in the kitchen. And now, we're losing our grasp on how it works under the hood as we delegate more and more to the agents.

But I'd never go back to the way software used to be written. Give me process isolation and online updates. Give me higher-level programming languages that abstract common pitfalls from C and C++. Give me game designers that handle timing using the system clock. Give me Steam and Windows Update. You can keep your old release process that fell by the wayside.

[0]

From what I remember from trying to install Debian in my high school years, the most popular app on Linux was anything that could edit XF86Config.

[1]

I'm having trouble corroborating this anecdote with information I can find online. The details might not be exactly right. But this is what happened, to the extent that the memory survived 25ish years.

[2]

Not GHz, MHz!

item.title: Python's experimental JIT to be removed (392 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://lwn.net/SubscriberLink/1102102/0c00e4d550f25f8c/, See on Hacker News

[+] Proceed to the article

Python's experimental just-in-time (JIT) compiler, which was added to CPython in 2024 for the 3.13 release, is on its way out. In June, the Python steering council announced that it was pausing work on the JIT in CPython's main branch until there was an accepted Python Enhancement Proposal (PEP) that addressed concerns about maintenance, compatibility, and set clear success metrics as well as a timeline for completion. After creating PEP 836 ("JIT Go Brrr: The Path to a Supported JIT Compiler for CPython") to try to meet the council's request, and after months of discussion, the JIT maintainers have withdrawn the PEP. For now, it appears that development on the once-promising project has come to an end.

The JIT was added to CPython by Brandt Bucher in early 2024. Generally, such a major feature would be expected to land only after the council had approved a standards-track PEP. Bucher had given a talk (YouTube video, slides) about the JIT at a Python core developer sprint, and announced his intent to merge the feature—but he had not taken the step of authoring or submitting a PEP for its approval. He was prodded into doing so by steering council member Thomas Wouters, who was also serving as the release manager for Python 3.13.

Bucher and Savannah Ostrowski drafted PEP 744 ("JIT Compilation"), which was an informational PEP—meaning it only provides information to the Python community and does not represent formal consensus to proceed on a feature or project. LWN covered the discussion of PEP 744 in April 2024, and later covered Bucher's talk on the JIT at PyCon US 2024, as well as the follow-up talk at PyCon US 2025.

PEP it up

Work on the JIT had been proceeding on the basis of PEP 744 until this June, when the council had put forward its formal request for the JIT maintainers to create a standards-track PEP. One might wonder, as Antoine Pitrou did, why the council had decided that it was time to speak up and ask for a new PEP. Wouters said that there was no "single triggering event for this request", but that the council had been discussing the topic for a while and indicated that it was looking to ensure the JIT work did not interfere with other projects. "There's been work trying to get the JIT to play nice with instrumentation, debugging, and profiling. There's also external JITs (like CinderX), JIT-adjacent things (like Numba and PyTorch's compile), and discussions about a tier 3 JIT." The council had waited until after the Python 3.15 beta release "to be clear that we're OK with the status quo for 3.15".

The council asked for a PEP that would make the case for the JIT "as a supported, non-experimental part of CPython: its guarantees, its maintenance commitments, and its impact on redistributors". The council set a deadline of six months for the PEP to be submitted and accepted; failing that, the council would require the JIT code to be removed from the CPython main branch.

Bucher, Ostrowski, and Ken Jin drafted PEP 836 and published it on the Python forum for community feedback on July 3. It generated quite a bit of discussion, some favorable and some critical. One of the key themes in the comments, such as this one by Wouters, and this comment by Mark Shannon, was that the draft felt like it should be two separate PEPs. Shannon, for example, thought that the PEP should only cover goals for accepting the JIT work and felt that it should leave out implementation details. There were also quite a few calls for additional information.

Bucher pushed back a bit on the suggestion that it should be two PEPs, and Ostrowski defended the structure of the PEP as it was. "Outlining goals like we have in the PEP without being able to share the plan and everything we've thought through alongside it would make me uncomfortable. To me, goals without plans behind them aren't really goals at all."

When we last looked at this topic in September, the discussion about the PEP had slowed down without a commitment to develop new PEPs or a formal statement from the council. The last word from the council at that time, in the form of a summary of its August 6 meeting, was that it had met with the PEP authors and was "discussing the state of the PEP and whether it answered the questions the SC asked in its request for a PEP".

Experimentation in main

On September 21, Wouters posted a statement from the steering council, minus Ostrowski (who is currently a member of the steering council but did not participate since she is a co-author of the PEP), that summarized its position. The statement said that PEP did answer all of the questions that were highlighted in the council's request, "although perhaps some less convincingly than others".

The council wished to make clear that it was not looking for the criteria that the JIT should meet to be a supported feature, or whether it should be considered such. Instead, the council was evaluating whether the JIT should continue as an experiment in CPython's main branch.

Part of the problem with allowing experimentation in main is the lack of unified design, and the uncertainty that core developers, package maintainers and users face as the experimentation changes behaviours and API surfaces.

The council said that the PEP was not specific enough about support plans, performance criteria, and too vague or too optimistic about a number of other areas. The statement included a ten-point list of items that the council wanted "to see either spelled out in the PEP, or at least discussed and rejected". The council's list expressed concerns ranging from memory impact to security. For example, on the topic of platform parity, the council wanted to ensure that the JIT was designed to be easily adopted for new platforms. It wanted assurance that the JIT's design would not be tied to specific platform or require platform-specific knowledge to maintain.

Another area that the council called out was user impact. It said that the PEP was "overly optimistic" about user-visible differences with the JIT enabled. There were many cases where users depend on idiosyncrasies in the interpreter design, "as we've seen with other Python implementations or even just between major Python versions", and it wanted clarification on how those differences would be handled. Would they be considered bugs, how would situations be handled if a difference in behavior was unavoidable, and so on.

Security was "an underserved area in the PEP", according to the council; it suggested that a discussion with the Python security response team was in order and that a security review should be part of the criteria for supported status as well.

PEP 836 specified a compatibility review milestone to correspond with the first Python 3.17 release candidate—which would be expected sometime in August 2028—that would involve running the test suites of the top PyPI packages to see if the JIT broke them. The council wanted that timeline moved up significantly. "We think that's way, way too late, and the compatibility review should be an ongoing and continuous process starting as soon as possible".

The council also worried about the JIT's design decisions being made "without critical review by the larger group of developers ultimately responsible for [CPython] development, maintenance and support". The bottom line, it said, was that PEP 836 "mostly answers the questions we asked" with no missing pieces, but it wanted more discussion on those topics so it could "gauge community support and consensus before we're asked to pronounce on this PEP".

Jin replied a few days later to thank the council for its detailed feedback and said that the group would work on its suggestions.

Withdrawn

After some consideration, it appears, the PEP's authors have decided not to continue pursing the council's approval. On October 19, Ostrowski (who is also release manager for Python 3.16 and 3.17) announced that the PEP was being withdrawn:

The Steering Council rightly sets a high bar for a proposal of this scope, and we don't feel we have the personal bandwidth to carry the current version forward. We continue to believe in the technical direction outlined in the PEP, including free-threaded support and a method-based frontend, and remain optimistic about the JIT's potential in CPython. We'll make the reference implementation available and link it from the withdrawn PEP so others who are interested can explore and build on that.

Barry Scott asked if that meant that work on the JIT was stopped. Brett Cannon replied that the work would be stopped in the main repository, but it would be up to the community whether the work would continue elsewhere. Dunc Graham suggested that there might be time for an alternative PEP to be submitted before the council's deadline. Cannon said that was not likely, "as all the people actively driving the JIT were either authors on that PEP or contributors to it".

With the PEP withdrawn, the JIT will likely be removed from CPython main fairly soon to ensure that any problems caused by its removal can be addressed early in the Python 3.16 development cycle. It is unclear whether the original drivers of the JIT work intend to continue working on it at all, or if it will simply be left for others to pick up if there is enough community interest. I have emailed the PEP authors for clarification, but have not yet received a reply.

item.title: Wikipedia's Cleanup of AI-Generated Content (400 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://spectrum.ieee.org/wikipedia-wikiproject-ai-writing-cleanup, See on Hacker News

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI?

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

item.title: AI promised less work. I've never worked more (602 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://oioannou.com/blog/ai-promised-less-work/, See on Hacker News

The pitch was that AI would give us our time back. Write less boilerplate, delegate the boring parts, go home earlier.

I am not complaining about the tools. I use agents for all of my engineering work now, and I wrote about how that setup evolved and why I still read the code. I can investigate and ship things that would not have been worth starting two years ago.

But somewhere this year I noticed that I am working more than I ever have, and that it feels heavier than it used to. Not because any single task is harder. Because there are so many more of them, all at once.

This post is me trying to understand that, with some data from my own GitHub history.

The old load and the new load

As a full-stack engineer, a normal week for me meant two or three serious tasks. A feature, a tricky bug, maybe a migration. Each one needed real focus, but I could hold one of them in my head at a time, finish it, and move to the next.

Today my week looks completely different. I have several agents running in parallel: one implementing a change, one investigating a production question, one working through a review, another doing research I will need later. None of them needs me all the time. Every one of them needs me sometimes.

That “sometimes” is the problem.

Each agent eventually comes back with a question, a plan to approve, a diff to read or a result to make sense of. Responding means switching contexts: reloading a different problem, a different repository and a different set of decisions.

Two or three serious tasks a week was tiring in a familiar way. Working with many agents is tiring in a new way. My attention is spread across more problems, and I find moving between them much more mentally draining.

What my GitHub history shows

I pulled my GitHub contribution calendar for every month from January 2019 to today and marked my roles at Bold.org, which I joined in January 2020: Full Stack Engineer until August 2022, Principal Engineer until August 2025, and Vice President of Technology since then. These are GitHub’s contribution counts, including private work, so they mix commits, pull requests, reviews and issues. It is a rough signal of activity, not a measure of value. 2019 is an incomplete baseline: my job before Bold.org used a self-hosted GitLab, so GitHub only shows what I did outside it. But the shape is hard to ignore.

The first part of the curve is what I expected:

  • My busiest coding years at Bold.org were the early ones. 2020 was my highest year, with 2,711 contributions. 2021 dropped to 1,839 and 2022 to 1,498.
  • The Principal Engineer years were flat and lower. From August 2022 to July 2025 I averaged 114 contributions a month, against 173 as a Full Stack Engineer. My lowest year was 2023, with 1,189.
  • The first months as VP of Technology looked the same. From August to December 2025 I averaged 111 a month, and December 2025 was my quietest month since joining Bold.org, with 50.

As a Principal Engineer, more of my work went into architecture, deep dives into concepts, setting up projects and planning, rather than fixing bugs or iterating on features. Becoming VP of Technology continued that shift, with even less feature work expected. At least until AI came along.

Then 2026 happened:

  • I am back at my Full Stack Engineer pace. By October 27 I am at 2,102 contributions, already more than any full year from 2021 to 2025. Over the same period in 2020 I had 2,371, so 2026 is close to my busiest year but not above it.
  • August 2026 is the busiest month in the whole timeline. 427 contributions, against a previous high of 319 in April 2020.
  • My normal day moved back up. The median weekday was 3 or 4 contributions every year from 2022 to 2025. In 2026 it is 7, close to the 8 I had in 2020.
  • Fewer weekdays without GitHub activity. Through October 27, I had 18 weekdays with zero contributions, compared with 40–46 across each full year from 2022 to 2025. These are days without recorded GitHub activity, not days off work.
  • Heavy days became routine again. From 2022 to 2025 I had exactly one day per year with 24 or more contributions. In 2026 I already have 16, almost the 17 I had in all of 2020.

Almost all of this is private work. The dashed line in the chart is public contributions only: it was near zero from 2021 to 2025 and came back this year, with 191 so far, but that is still less than a tenth of 2026.

The twist is the role. In 2020 I was a full-stack engineer doing feature work full time, and this is roughly what that looked like on GitHub. Today I lead engineering at Bold.org and do far less feature work than I used to. On paper my graph should look like my Principal Engineer years, or lower. Instead it is back where it was when writing code was my whole job.

What changed is how much work feels worth taking on. When coding is cheap, I can fix bugs I would previously have left alone, improve patterns across the codebase, take on new projects and turn more ideas into something real. Much of this is work I would never have considered before. Agents did not just make my existing workload faster to finish. They made it easy to give myself a much bigger one.

Bursts, then burnout

Looking at the monthly totals, 2026 is not one steady climb. It is a series of bursts.

January and February were the first clear burst, with 277 and 233 contributions. This is when I started working seriously with agents, and when the observability experiment that became our internal company agent took off. Every week revealed something new I could suddenly delegate, and I wanted to try all of it.

March to June generally winds down, from 203 contributions in March to 77 in June. But April was a smaller burst along the way, another month when I had ideas and acted on them. I think improvements in the models were part of that renewed energy. Its monthly total of 187 is below January to March, but it includes a 29-contribution day and 68 public contributions, my highest public total of the year.

August is the biggest burst of all. Coming back from my summer break, the calendar shows a full week of zero contributions in early August. Then every weekday from August 10 to August 27 was between 14 and 43. August ended at 427 contributions, the busiest month in the whole timeline. September stayed high at 301.

Every cycle starts the same way. A new model or a new workflow makes something possible that was not possible last month, and my head fills with ideas. Because implementation is now cheap, there is no natural friction stopping me from pursuing all of them at once. So I do. I start more agents, open more threads and say yes to more experiments.

That works for a few weeks. Then the reviewing and context switching catch up with me, and I pull back to a more stable flow. I stay there until something exciting comes along, or until a holiday recharges me enough that I go straight back into another burst.

I count three of these cycles since January.

At the end of a burst, I feel tired of AI. I do not want to start another agent or think of more ideas. I do my normal work, but I stop chasing the extra projects and possibilities because I do not have the mental bandwidth for them.

The low season is not low anymore

The part that surprised me most is not the peaks. It is how much I am doing between them.

March did not feel like the bursts in January, February or August, but I was still doing substantial work. It had 203 contributions, against my Principal Engineer average of 114 a month. I was still acting on ideas, but that level of activity no longer felt like an exceptional push. Even when I think I am taking it easy, there are still agent results to work through, reviews to finish and small things that are now “just a quick prompt”.

June was genuinely low, with 77 contributions, comparable to my quieter Principal Engineer months. Maybe that was when all the tiredness caught up with me. Not every quiet month is higher than before. But outside the bursts, I still find myself taking on more work than I used to. That is what I mean by the low season not feeling low anymore.

Where that leaves me

AI made room for work I would never have considered before. I like being able to fix more things and turn more ideas into something real. But the capacity to implement those ideas has grown much faster than my capacity to think about them. Eventually I stop wanting to start another agent and go back to just doing my normal work. I have not figured out a balance. For now, I am noticing that being able to do more keeps turning into doing more. And I am tired.

A note on how this article was written: AI helped me pull and analyze my GitHub contribution data, build the chart and draft this article. The experience, decisions and opinions are mine.

item.title: Roblox downloaded 145GB models from us (including adult content) without asking (432 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://open3dlab.com/news/roblox-downloaded-145-gb-of-models-from-our-sites/, See on Hacker News

On 15 and 16 October 2026, a crawler that said it belonged to Roblox walked through almost every project on Open3DLab, SFMLab and SmutBase, and proceeded to download complete copies of 1,027 files from 712 projects. 145.5 GB of our creators' work, downloaded for what we assume are AI training purposes.

This post briefly describes what happened, what mitigations were taken, and what this signals for the community at large. A more detailed writeup outlining what we saw in our logs will be posted at a later time.

What happened

On Sunday the 18th of October, we noticed a crawler making a large number of requests to our sites and download infrastructure. The crawler sent the same user agent on every request, trellis2-data-sourcing/1.0 (3D foundation model research; [redacted]@roblox.com). It came from a single Amazon Web Services (AWS) address. It had read the main page of 18,926 projects, which is practically our entire catalogue, in 26,429 requests over a span of 34 hours.

After pulling the project pages, it downloaded complete copies of 1,027 files from 712 projects, 145.5 GB in all, before suspending operations during the weekend. The downloads include 364 files (54.8 GB) from 224 projects on SmutBase, which hosts adult content only. With the SFMLab projects marked adult, 345 of the 712 projects (62.6 GB) are adult content.

The main limiting factor in the number of files downloaded was the crawler's reliance on the free download servers, which have caps on speed limit and number of concurrent downloads. The crawler did not respect our robots.txt, (which it did retrieve), ignored our Terms of Service, (which forbid scraping), and defied the creators' licenses: 423 of the 712 projects are licensed for non-commercial use only. Within the sample it retrieved, it took adult projects at the same rate as everything else. Some examples include models of Eve from Stellar Blade, Mei from Overwatch, and a Horse cock dildo.

Our response

We found it on 18 October and blocked further attempts the same morning. The scraper had suspended its activity by that point, and we did not notice any scraper that weekend. We emailed the address in its user agent on 18 October and asked Roblox for comment. We have not had a reply.

The crawler resumed scraping activity on October 19th, with all requests getting blocked by our servers. The scraper did not reduce its download attempts when faced with our blocks, and the scrapes seemed to fit neatly within office hours, only briefly pausing for an hour around lunchtime, and ending activity around the end of the workday (CEST). On the 20th, their scraper made its final return at 8:00, slowly tapering requests from lunchtime onward, likely in an effort to test our rate limiting. The requests stopped around 15:00. We sent another email to Roblox for questions, to which they again did not reply.

Speculation

This section contains our speculation and assumptions based on public information, and the information we noticed in our logs.

Roblox has been building a "3D foundation model" since at least 2025.In March 2025 Roblox introduced Cube, which it calls its core generative AI system for 3D and 4D. The accompanying paper describes the goal as a foundation model for 3D intelligence. It lists character rigging among the things that model should eventually do, and generating characters and avatars as future work. Its first shape model was trained on roughly 1.5 million 3D assets from licensed and public datasets such as Objaverse, plus free assets from Roblox's own Creator Store whose creators had opted in. In February 2026 Roblox began rolling out "4D generation" built on Cube.

The address in the user agent belongs to a researcher who is among the 40-plus authors of that Cube paper. The researcher's public professional profile says they are building a 3D foundation model at Roblox, and their earlier published work is on 3D reconstruction and real-time 3D rendering. We want to be clear: we don't suggest this researcher did anything on their own initiative or out of the ordinary for their job. A data-collection run like this is a company's decision, and the responsibility for it is Roblox's. But the profile says what the user agent says: the people behind this crawler build 3D foundation models.

The "trellis2" in trellis2-data-sourcing may refer to TRELLIS.2, an open 3D generation model Microsoft released in late 2025. It may mean the data was meant for training or tuning a model like it, or it may just be a project codename. We don't know. What we can say is that TRELLIS.2's published data toolkit contains no web crawler and no user agent, so this crawler and its label were written for the job. It is also possible that Roblox is re-using the Trellis.2 tooling for its own foundational model and it is re-using these scripts for its next model; the tools are open source.

Our sites are full of things a 3D model-generation system needs and public datasets have relatively little of: complete, textured characters, many of them rigged, in the formats artists actually work in, each with a title, a description and preview images.

Put together, we think the most likely explanation is that the crawler was collecting training or evaluation data for Roblox's 3D foundation model work. We can't prove it, and we don't know whether any of our creators' files ended up in a model.

Roblox's track record

This isn't the first time Roblox has been criticised for how it treats the people whose work its platform runs on, or for how it handles other people's rights.

  • Young developers. In 2021 the games outlet People Make Games published a video investigation arguing that Roblox turns its young users into underpaid developers. By its calculation Roblox kept around 75% of the money spent in developers' games, against Steam's 30%, and paid creators in Robux, which they can only cash out once they've earned a minimum amount. Roblox declined to discuss its revenue share and payout minimums. (In September 2025 it raised its cash-out rate by 8.5%.)
  • Copyright. In 2021 the US National Music Publishers' Association sued Roblox for at least $200 million over unlicensed music on the platform. The case settled later that year for an undisclosed amount.
  • Child safety. In October 2024 the short seller Hindenburg Research accused Roblox of inflating its user numbers and of failing to protect children. Roblox called the report misleading and pointed out that its authors stood to profit from a falling share price. Since then the attorneys general of Louisiana, Kentucky, Texas and Florida, among other states, have sued Roblox over child safety, and private lawsuits have been consolidated in US federal court. These are allegations, not findings.

None of this proves anything about the crawler, but it strengthens our opinion that Roblox is a deeply unethical business. It shows a company that has repeatedly been accused of putting growth ahead of the people its platform depends on.

You see how this looks, right?

More than a third of Roblox's daily users were under 13 in 2025, by its own figures. Its rules ban sexual content, and in 2025 it tightened them further.

Roblox's crawler took 224 projects from a site called SmutBase, which describes itself as exclusively for adult content, and 121 more that are marked adult on SFMLab. It took them at the same rate as everything else: 345 of the 712 projects it downloaded from are adult content. The further scraping attempts did not discriminate between adult content either.

We want to be careful here. We don't think Roblox set out to collect adult content, and we have no evidence that any of it reached a model or a product. The scrapes were likely automated. But that is exactly the problem: as far as our logs show, nobody checked. A crawler working for a company whose platform tens of millions of children use was pointed at an adult site, and it took explicit models without telling them apart from anything else.

Models reproduce what they learn from. If adult training data reaches a model that generates assets for Roblox, the only thing between that data and children is whatever filter Roblox builds afterwards, because its data collection didn't filter anything. Furthermore, when a creator deletes a project, or we remove one for breaking our rules or after a copyright notice, it's gone from our sites, but remains in these datasets. One project the crawler took has already been disabled on SFMLab since. If Roblox still has its copy, that copy is still there.

We're not against adult content. It's our bread and butter. We think consenting adults should be able to access and enjoy this content freely, without the government looking over their shoulder. What we object to is our adult sites being emptied into an exploitative gaming company's training data without anyone asking, and being mixed into content offered to literal children.

For a company being sued by several US states over child safety, "our AI team bulk-downloaded an adult site without looking" is not a good position to be in.

If the penalty for a crime is a fine, then that law only exists for the lower class.

This section is opinion.

Roblox isn't the worst offender in AI's appetite for other people's work, just the latest to turn up in our logs. It isn't the only AI company in them, either. In the month before we found trellis2-data-sourcing, Meta's AI crawler, Meta-ExternalAgent, made about 380,000 requests to our sites, almost all from Meta's own network, and loaded 211,000 project pages. We have since blocked their crawler as well.

The Roblox trellis2 crawler is the first individual crawler we spotted that actually pulled assets uploaded by our users, in flagrant defiance of any copyright or license that might apply to it. It fits a broader context, of AI labs taking content without permission. Here's what the largest companies have been accused of, and in some cases have admitted:

  • Meta downloaded at least 81.7 TB of pirated books by torrent from shadow libraries, including through Anna's Archive, according to court filings by the authors suing it. In June 2025 a judge ruled that training on the books was fair use on that record, while stressing that the ruling didn't make Meta's conduct lawful in general.
  • Meta, again: the adult studio Strike 3 Holdings alleges that Meta torrented thousands of its films to train AI video models. Meta says the downloads were for individuals' "personal use". In June 2026 the court refused to dismiss the case. The irony is hard to miss: Strike 3 is best known for suing thousands of individual BitTorrent users.
  • Nvidia contacted Anna's Archive about high-speed access to its collection of pirated books for training data, and management signed off soon after, according to an amended class-action complaint filed in January 2026. Nvidia argued that contacting a pirate site isn't infringement. The court has since largely refused to dismiss the case.
  • Anthropic downloaded hundreds of thousands of pirated books. A judge found that training on books it had bought was fair use, but keeping a library of pirated copies was not. In July 2026 the court approved a $1.5 billion settlement, about $3,000 per book.

Now compare how copyright treats everyone else. In the early 2000s Jammie Thomas-Rasset was ordered to pay $222,000 for sharing 24 songs. Internet activist Aaron Swartz faced federal charges carrying decades in prison for downloading academic articles. The Internet Archive, a nonprofit library, lost in court for lending scanned copies of books it owned. Meanwhile, the Internet Archive's online library gets repeatedly scanned by AI companies in return.

We'll be honest about where we stand. We don't like copyright as it exists. We'd like to see it radically reformed, and we wouldn't mourn it if it were abolished. Our community lives in its grey areas every day: many of the models on our sites are fan ports of characters from commercial games, made out of love and shared for free. When a studio sends us a takedown notice, we comply.

While we as small artists and fan communities get copyright used against us, the world's largest companies are committing copyright infringement at a scale unseen in human history. This has been the case since the invention of the internet of course; digital media make duplication, remixing and resharing trivial, but copyright law never caught up. Filesharing stabbed copyright in the gut. AI is just twisting the knife, and completes the creation an unequal system where copyright infringement is only a crime if you're a low net worth individual.

So we aren't asking for stricter copyright laws, or stronger protection for copyright holders. That will only benefit the major entertainment companies like Disney and Adobe who have already stacked the deck in their favor, and are happily making deals with Big-Tech and crushing small creators in the process. We're pointing out that the copyright we have isn't applied equally, and is in practice a two tier system. Individuals face ruinous damages for minor infractions. The largest companies in the world face a cost to be negotiated after the fact, if anyone can afford to sue them. A law that only works downwards gives nobody a reason to respect it, and it can't last in this form.

For time being, we'd like to ask Roblox to respect the norms of this community. You credit people. You respect the license they chose. If you want to use someone's work for something they didn't offer it for, you ask. Those norms cost nothing to follow, and Roblox's crawler followed none of them. This scrape attempt saturated the connections for our free download servers for a couple of days, causing problems for our community of legitimate human users. It shows a lack of respect for the people who make this site what it is. those who produced, shared and host the work that you were about to throw in your AI mixer.

Questions for Roblox

We're sad that the emails we sent to Roblox were not met with a timely response, and would thus like to publicly ask Roblox for its response. These are the questions we'd like Roblox to answer:

  1. Did Roblox run the trellis2-data-sourcing crawler?
  2. What was the data for? Has any of it been used to train or evaluate a model, and if so, which?
  3. Why did the crawler ignore our robots.txt rules and our Terms of Service?
  4. Did anyone review which sites the crawler would visit? Was adult content excluded at any stage?
  5. Will Roblox delete the files and anything derived from them, and confirm that in writing?
  6. Will Roblox respect our creators' license choices, NonCommercial in particular, from now on?

We hope Roblox reaches out to us. Also, if you are a person with information on what Roblox is doing, or a fellow site owner who has been targeted, feel free to get in touch as well. We're eager to hear if there's more of a pattern to the scraper's behavior.

We've kept the full export of the relevant log files for auditing by external parties if the need arises.

About us

Open3DLab, SFMLab and SmutBase are three community sites for free 3D resources, run by a small team. SFMLab started in 2014 for Source Filmmaker models. SmutBase followed in 2016 and is exclusively for adult content. Open3DLab, for general-purpose 3D work, joined in 2020. Creators upload characters, props, maps and environments, choose a license for each project, and anyone can download the files for free. All three sites are intended for adults only.

About the redaction. The email address in the user agent is a Roblox employee's work address. We've removed the name: this article is about what the Roblox crawler did, not about one person.

About Attribution. We take the user agent at face value. Anyone can type any email address into a user agent, and the crawler ran from Amazon's cloud, not from Roblox's own network. Nothing we've seen suggests impersonation, and the label fits Roblox's published research closely. Still, it is a self-description, and it's the first thing we'd like Roblox to confirm.

item.title: Gforth 1.0 (134 pts)
item.description:
URL: https://gforth.org/manual/1.0/NEWS.html, See on Hacker News

User-visible changes between Gforth 0.7.x and 1.0:

Many of the words below are just mentioned, without much indication what they do. You can find out more by klicking on the word in the Web version of this document, by typing "help " in Gforth, or by clicking on the word in the word index.

This text mentions words that appear the first time in the documentation; some have been available earlier, but were not documented.

Stability

It is now documented which words are intended to be permanently supported, and which are not; see Stability Goals.

Headline features

  • The text interpreter can recognize more things:

    • Additional ways to write literals in source code: scaled notation for FP numbers (6k5, 23%); strings ("string"), xts ( `word), nts ( ``word), body addresses (<word> <word+8>). See Literals in source code;
    • You can specify the vocabulary (or several) of a word, e.g., forth:and vs. assembler:and.
    • Nonparsing syntax for dealing with value-flavoured and defer-flavoured words (v and d in the following examples): ->v for to v; +>v for +to v; 'v for addr v; @>d for action-of d; =>d for is d. See rec-to.
    • Contents of environment variables: ${LANG}
    • You can extend the text interpreter with more recognizers: recs rec-name rec-local rec-scope rec-number .-is-dcell? rec-float rec-complex rec-string rec-to rec-dtick rec-tick rec-body rec-env rec-meta rec-forth rec-sequence: get-recs set-recs rec-none translate-name translate-cell translate-dcell translate-float translate-complex translate-string scan-translate-string translate-env translate-to rec-filter rec-forth-nt? translate: interpreting compiling postponing ?rec-found

  • IDE features:

    • Show source code of a word (locate browse).
    • show uses of a word (where nw bw ww).
    • backtraces show source locations and can be browsed (nt bt tt);
    • and use an editor if desired (edit g gg whereg);
    • other words: fancy-after-l xt-locate l n b before-locate after-locate ll short-where expand-where prepend-where unused-words

  • "Smart .s: ... guesses what stack items mean and displays them appropriately. .s itself stays dumb.

  • A status line at the bottom of the terminal shows BASE, stacks, and search order. -status +status

  • Multi-Tasking on multiple cores or hardware threads: newtask task newtask4 stacksize stacksize4 initiate execute-task kill-task kill stop stop-ns stop-dns thread-deadline halt sleep wake restart pause auser uallot up@ user' 's mutex lock unlock critical-section atomic!@ atomic+!@ atomic?!@ barrier

    Message queues (similar to the actor model) provide a way to combine communication with synchronization of the tasks: send-event ?events event-loop

    Cilk is useful for distributing work across tasks: cores cilk-init spawn spawn1 spawn2 cilk-sync cilk-bye

  • C interface enhancements, includig callbacks: c-value c-variable c-funptr c++-library-name c++-library add-libpath add-framework add-incdir add-cflags add-ldflags c-callback c-callback-thread callback#

  • The dictionary can now have more than one section, each with its own dictionary pointer, which allows allocation without affecting other sections, used, e.g., for nested definitions. See Sections. Words: next-section previous-section extra-section .sections

  • Postpone multiple words with ]]...[[.
